newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr dips as sun sets on samurais.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr dips as sun sets on samurais.

text.p: The Australian dollar sagged below 79 cents Tuesday as investors finally lost patience with its failure to extend a three week old rally past key resistance.

Bulls had been quietly confident that buying for a much heralded 50 billion yen dual currency samurai issue from IBM would clear away offers around US$0.7935. But frowns began to gather as, contrary to expectations, Japanese investors sold non-stop and were joined by U.S. and Asian speculators.
Exporter bids were limiting the losses for the moment, but dealers suspected a retreat to US$0.7850 was possible if fresh samurai demand did not apear soon and in size.
By 4.30 pm (0630 GMT) the dollar was feeling unwanted at US$0.7888/93 after fading from early US$0.7903/08 and Monday's late US$0.7910/15.

Traders noted the setback was minor given that the currency remained far above the US$0.7680 low struck in the wake of the July 31 rate cut. Overall, sentiment remained positive and only a break of the pivotal US$0.7810 chart level would change that.
On the crosses, the currency slid to 84.90/00 yen from 85.42/52 due to the selling out of Tokyo and a lapse in US$/yen.
It also eased to 1.1629/42 marks from 1.1699/1710 late Monday and to 57.7 on its trade weighted index from 57.9.
Traders said the market looked to be lightening short yen positions as a precautionary move ahead of a crucial report on the Japanese economy Wednesday.
They feared the Bank of Japan survey of business confidence might show the recovery progressing better than expected which in turn would rekindle speculation of a policy tightening there.

Analysts here are looking for the Tankan's main diffusion index of manufacturing to improve to around +1.0 in Q3 from -3.0 the quarter before and -12.0 in February. That would hardly be indicative of a booming economy, however, and they expected the non-manufacturing sector to retain a pessimistic outlook.
Japanese public sector spending was also on the wane and it was unclear how consumers would react to recent rises in mortgage rates and the prospect of higher sales taxes next year.
"These uncertanties are likely to continue to cloud the assessment by policymakers of the strength on private demand up to early 1997," said Macquarie Bank economist Richard Gibbs.
"So the Tankan alone is unlikely to spur monetary authorities to adopt a tighter policy stance."
That would be just as well for the local dollar since its yield advantage had already been impaired by last month's surprise cut in Australian rates.
And the risk of another easing remains a real one, although many felt it would depend on how economic data, particularly on employment and wages, pans out for the next two to three months.

Nevertheless, the Reserve Bank's policy-making committee holds its monthly meeting next week and there are whispers governor Bernie Fraser had wanted to cut rates by a full 1.00 point last month but was persuaded to hold 0.50 point back.

The more Machiavellian in the market noted that this would be Fraser's last meeting before he retires, so he could favour an immediate easing on his authority thus leaving the slate clean for his successor Ian Macfarlane.
Macfarlane, they reckoned, wanted to be seen as an inflation hawk and might not want a cut for his first action as governor.
Today's quarterly balance of payments figures were rendered largely obsolete by the early relerase of June quarter GDP data which showed net exports detracted 0.9 point from GDP-E.

The figures showed the quarterly current account deficit was partly financed by A$3.62 billion of foreign debt which helped analysts narrow their forecasts for June quarter net foreign debt, released Wednesday. They are now looking for debt to widen slightly to around A$187.00 billion from A$184.8 billion in Q1.
